about: In brief: a short summary shown at the end of a piece in the EPRIS app. Keyed by article id. Each text is a plain English string or {"EN": …, "UA": …}. Set "hidden": true to pull one.

97.name: Yayoi Kusama
97.who: Japanese artist, 1929–2026; painter, sculptor and maker of rooms
did: Infinity Nets: huge canvases of tiny looping strokes, painted in New York from 1958
Soft sculptures and the first mirrored room, Phalli’s Field (1965)
Narcissus Garden at the 1966 Venice Biennale: 1,500 mirrored balls, sold at $2 each
The Obliteration Room (2002), which visitors cover with coloured dots
The yellow pumpkin on Naoshima, rebuilt in 2022 after a typhoon
97.why: She made the most repeatable picture in the art world and it never wore out. Her last retrospective is at the Stedelijk, Amsterdam, until 17 January 2027.
97.new: Instead of showing infinity on a canvas, she built rooms that put the viewer inside it – small, multiplied, and not afraid.

96.name: Ryoji Ikeda
96.who: Japanese composer and visual artist, born in Gifu in 1966; works in Paris and Kyoto
did: Records of pure sine tones and glitches; matrix won the Golden Nica at Ars Electronica (2001)
spectra: 49 searchlights forming one column of light, in Hobart (2013) and over the Thames (2014)
test pattern: any data turned into barcode stripes laid across a floor
A residency at CERN (2014–15), then supersymmetry and micro | macro
data-verse, a trilogy built from NASA, CERN and Human Genome Project data
96.why: Winner of the 2026 Nam June Paik Prize; a solo exhibition follows at the Nam June Paik Art Center in 2027.
96.new: Most data art decorates its numbers. Ikeda strips a data set to its simplest signal – a stripe, a dot, a tone – and makes it so large you stand inside it.

94.name: Tomás Saraceno
94.who: Argentine artist and trained architect, born in Tucumán in 1973; based in Berlin
did: Cloud Cities: habitable structures you climb into, among them one on the roof of the Met (2012)
Arachnophilia: research with scientists into how spiders build and sense through silk
Aerocene: a balloon flown by sunlight alone rose 272 metres in 2020 and set 32 world records
The Sanctuary of Water, built with eleven Indigenous communities of Salinas Grandes
94.why: His largest show in Germany, Ancestral Futures, is at Haus der Kunst, Munich, until 7 February 2027.
94.new: His utopias can be measured: a balloon in metres, a flush in litres, a sanctuary in whether the people who asked for it will keep it.

93.name: Javier Ordóñez
93.who: Basque painter and sculptor, born in Bilbao in 1960; studios in Bilbao and Cantabria
did: Escorias de Hierro (Iron Slag): paintings and sculpted Blocks in honour of the miners and foundry workers of Bizkaia, his great-grandfather among them
Figuraciones Cromáticas: landscapes of Cantabria, Lanzarote and the Asón valley reduced to masses of colour
Migraciones (2025): both series together, more than sixty works, at La Vidriera, Camargo
themes: sand, rust and slag as paint
tiredness as an engine for change
93.why: He carries the Basque abstract tradition – Oteiza, Chillida, Sistiaga – into the materials of Bizkaia’s own industry.
93.new: The paint itself is the memory: tinted sand, metal powder and Corten steel rust on handmade stretchers, so the work is the residue of the work it remembers.

92.name: Rosaria Valenti
92.who: Self-taught abstract painter from Stoke-on-Trent, now in Somerset, with Sicilian roots
did: Paints without a plan: starts from a feeling, makes a mark and answers the canvas
Within, a journey in three parts: Held, Unbound, Echo
Freedom, the painting she will never part with, made after a hard time in her family’s life
themes: joy and darkness in one frame
92.why: Her paintings show how abstraction can hold a feeling too hard to put into words – and leave the viewer feeling a little less alone.
92.new: Nothing is thrown away: covered marks stay in the painting, “like old wounds that have healed”.

90.name: Akiko Hirai
90.who: Japanese-born potter, working in London for more than twenty years
did: Moon jars whose glaze cracks and lifts like river ice
Tall cylinders thrown with several centres, so they seem to sway
Kohiki pieces: white slip over dark clay that thins to show the body beneath
The exhibition Things that disappear when touched at Contemporary Ceramics, London (2026)
90.why: Her work belongs to the change that has taken pottery from ‘craft’ into the museum as sculpture.
90.new: She takes the moon jar’s old imperfection much further, until the jar looks caught in the middle of a geological event.
